title: Reversible vs. Irreversible Neuronal Injury in Brain Ischemia: Role of the Mitochondrial–Synaptic Axis
abstract: Ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury triggers a rapid and self-amplifying cascade of mitochondrial dysfunction, synaptic instability, and neuroinflammation that ultimately determines neuronal survival and functional recovery. Early bioenergetic collapse-driven by mitochondrial depolarization, Reactive oxygen species (ROS) overproduction, and impaired mitophagy-initiates excitotoxic signaling and calpain-mediated structural degradation at vulnerable synapses. These events converge with microglial and astrocytic activation to exacerbate cytokine release, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and delayed neuronal injury. Therapeutic strategies targeting this axis show considerable promise. Mitochondria-directed interventions-including mitophagy modulation, Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) inhibition, antioxidant nanocarriers, and emerging mitochondrial transplantation-restore Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, stabilize membrane potential, and prevent downstream excitotoxic injury. Synaptic protection via N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)/postsynaptic density protein-95 (PSD-95) uncoupling, α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptor stabilization, and calpain inhibition preserves dendritic architecture and neurotransmission. Modulation of inflammatory pathways, particularly Interleukin-1β (IL-1β), Tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and Interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling, as well as cell-specific microglial and astrocytic reprogramming, further attenuates secondary degeneration. Gene- and RNA-based therapies, nanoparticles engineered for BBB penetration, and extracellular vesicle-mediated delivery systems represent additional advanced platforms moving toward clinical translation. Despite substantial progress, challenges remain, including timing constraints, region-specific vulnerability (e.g., CA1 vs. CA3), limited BBB permeability, and species differences in mitochondrial dynamics and glial responses. Integrative multimodal strategies-combining mitochondrial repair, synaptic stabilization, and immunomodulation-along with advanced imaging, spatial transcriptomics, and patient-derived organoids, may accelerate the development of precision therapies for I/R injury. This review synthesizes mechanistic and translational evidence demonstrating that the mitochondria-synapse-inflammation axis forms a unified pathological framework across experimental and clinical I/R settings, including transient focal ischemia, global ischemia following cardiac arrest (CA), and reperfusion after thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
authors: Ki‐Yeon Yoo, Bo Hyun Jung, Ji Hyeon Ahn, Moo‐Ho Won

title: Electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging using a familial temporal lobe epilepsy model in cats: an exploratory methodological pilot study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Reliable methods for identifying the epileptogenic zone (EZ) in veterinary medicine remain limited. Although intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) is considered the most dependable approach for EZ localization, noninvasive simultaneous EEG and functional magnetic resonance imaging (EEG-fMRI) has been applied in human medicine as an alternative. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: Develop and evaluate EEG-fMRI methodology for clinical application in veterinary medicine and evaluate the methodological feasibility of EEG-fMRI using cats with familial spontaneous epilepsy (FSECs). ANIMALS: Ten cats with clear interictal epileptiform discharges on scalp EEG were selected from an FSEC colony with previously suggested amygdalo-hippocampal involvement. METHODS: Each cat underwent 3 scalp EEG and EEG-fMRI sessions. After preprocessing, blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) activation maps were generated. Primary analyses evaluated amygdalo-hippocampal activation using small-volume correction (SVC) and group-level analysis. RESULTS: The BOLD activation was detected in all sessions at an exploratory threshold, but no activation survived correction for multiple comparisons. The SVC analysis identified amygdalo-hippocampal activation in 16/30 sessions. Group-level analysis identified the largest cluster extending from the left parahippocampal gyrus to the hippocampal body. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: This exploratory pilot study showed that EEG-fMRI could be technically implemented in FSECs, but individual-level EZ localization remains insufficient for clinical use. Further optimization, data from surgical candidates, and multimodal comparisons are needed.
authors: Takayuki Miura, Rikako Asada, Daisuke Hasegawa

title: Toward A Whole-Brain Interface Enabled by High-Resolution Surface Electrophysiology
abstract: The goal of building a whole-brain interface - capable of generating a real-time digital representation of the state of the entire central nervous system - has long been framed as a hardware challenge of recording simultaneously from ever-larger numbers of microelectrodes. Advances in high-resolution neural interfaces now enable electrophysiologic interaction with the human nervous system at spatial and temporal resolutions previously unattainable without disrupting tissue architecture or physiology. These capabilities create new opportunities for mechanistic neuroscience, neuroprosthetics, and precision-guided neurosurgery. With the advent of modern microelectrode array technology, however, the whole-brain interface has also become a data challenge. Rather than pursuing large-scale human brain recording purely through a single device placed in a single patient, we demonstrate here that systematic multi-subject aggregation, across brain regions and behavioral paradigms, in a common anatomical framework, can achieve something functionally similar to a whole-brain interface. Here we present an approach to a functional atlas of the human central nervous system derived from high-resolution surface electrophysiology recordings obtained in the first 70 patients implanted with an anatomically conformal, thin-film neural interface positioned in more than 100 locations. The atlas comprises >100,000 electrode deployments and catalogs placement across a broad range of neuroanatomic targets spanning the motor, sensory, language, auditory, and associative domains, as well as brainstem and spinal cord structures that have historically been difficult to access at high electrophysiologic resolution. Across participants, aggregated recordings reveal somatotopic organization, including digit representations that follow a lateral-to-medial ordering consistent with classical homuncular maps, with transitions between adjacent representations occurring over spatial scales of approximately 0.8 - 2.0 mm; canonical frequency-band signatures, such as movement-related beta-band suppression and focal high-gamma (70 - 200 Hz) increases during motor and speech behaviors; and task-modulated population dynamics in both evoked and spontaneous activity across cortical, brainstem, and spinal cord regions. These findings yield insight into patterns of mesoscale electrophysiological dynamics conserved across the entire human central nervous system, suggesting that fine-scale functional organization is preserved across individuals when aligned to common anatomical landmarks. We further demonstrate several applications of these high-resolution recordings, including real-time neural decoding from upper extremity motor cortex to enable real-time neuroprosthetic control, and from ventrolateral cortex to decode cortical correlates of spoken language, facial movements, and complex facial expressions of emotion, supporting initial feasibility of combined verbal and nonverbal communication interfaces. Together, these results establish a paradigm for approaching large-scale interfaces with the human brain, as well as a starting point for a scalable, extensible atlas of human electrophysiologic function designed to accelerate discovery across basic neuroscience, translational research, and clinical neurotechnology.
authors: Elton Ho, Katrina Barth, Jacqueline Dister, Aneil Srivastava, Adam J. Poole et al.

title: Single-Neuron Mechanisms of Human Odor Processing
abstract: Our senses are the brain's window to the world. Organisms explore their environments through their senses. Understanding how sensory information is processed and integrated to form percepts and guide behavior is a fundamental goal of neuroscience. In this thesis, we investigate the neural coding principles underlying the sense of olfaction in humans. For this purpose, we leverage the rare opportunity to record from individual neurons in the human brain of patients undergoing invasive presurgical epilepsy diagnostics. To fully utilize these rare data, it is critical to optimize the quality of the recorded data. Here, we show that duplicate spike events can affect the overall quality of these data. Based on this, we develop an open-source algorithm that automatically identifies and eliminates such events, thereby enhancing the quality of human single-neuron recordings. Next, we apply these techniques to record the activity of individual neurons in the human olfactory system during an odor rating and identification task. Our recordings demonstrate how neurons in the human piriform cortex and medial temporal lobe encode odor identity, revealing distinct regional coding principles and effects of repetition suppression. We further describe how individual brain regions are involved in odor-related behavior, with amygdala neurons coding for odor valence and hippocampal representations predicting odor identification performance. Recording from the same neuronal population during presentation of odor-related images, we discover image-modulated neurons in the primary olfactory cortex (piriform cortex), and identify cross-modal coding at early stages of human olfactory processing. We even find neurons responding to the odor, image, and written word of a specific odor object (e.g., banana). Together, our results provide a detailed characterization of central odor processing at the single-neuron level in the human brain and lay the foundation for future research on human olfaction and cognition.
authors: Marcel S. Kehl

title: Mice detect and discriminate temporal patterns of mesoscale optogenetic cortical stimulation
abstract: ABSTRACT Optogenetic stimulation is widely used to establish causal links between neural activity, behavior, and sensory perception, yet animals may also perceive the neural stimulation itself, a phenomenon termed “optoception.” We hypothesized that cortical optogenetic stimulation would generate an artificial percept that could be distinguished from externally evoked sensations and characterized psychometrically in an operant task. We tested this hypothesis using mesoscale cortical photostimulation delivered by a 3 mm, 459 nm LED implanted over auditory cortex. Four mice expressing Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in excitatory neurons learned a head-fixed go/no-go task in which 20 Hz cortical photostimulation served as the target. ChR2-positive mice detected cortical photostimulation relative to LED-off catch trials, distinguished it from both an external LED matched in wavelength and pulse rate and from an acoustic noise matched in amplitude-modulation rate, and discriminated between 20- and 10-Hz cortical photostimulation. Reducing implanted-LED optical power initially lowered rate-discrimination sensitivity, which then increased across training sessions, demonstrating perceptual learning. In two mice tested with 11 randomly interleaved rates spanning 10-20 Hz, lick probability followed a saturating rate-dependent function. Two ChR2-negative littermates failed to acquire photostimulation-locked behavioral responding. Together, these findings show that mesoscale cortical optogenetic stimulation generates a graded, learnable artificial percept whose behavioral readout depends on photostimulation rate and optical power. This single-LED preparation provides a cost-efficient and wavelength-extensible platform for psychometric analysis of optoception. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Optogenetic stimulation can alter sensory processing, but the neural perturbation itself may also become a perceptual cue. We show that mice detect mesoscale cortical photostimulation delivered by a 3 mm implanted LED, distinguish it from matched external light and sound, and discriminate differences in photostimulation rate. When implanted-LED optical power was reduced, discrimination sensitivity initially declined and then increased across training sessions, revealing perceptual learning of optoception. Thus, mesoscale cortical photostimulation generates a graded internal signal whose behavioral readout depends on stimulation rate, optical power, and experience. A single implanted LED provides a cost- efficient and wavelength-extensible assay for measuring optogenetic perception.
authors: Gabrielle Stephens, Nikolas A. Francis

title: Pre-Clinical Evaluation and Standardized Scale-Up of a Novel Poly-Herbal Nootropic Compound for the Reversal of Age-Related Cognitive Frailty and Neuroinflammation
abstract: Abstract- Background: Age related cognitive frailty, characterized by neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, cholinergic deficit, and impaired synaptic integrity has limited disease modifying therapies. Nootropic research and development from traditional Ayurvedic medicines is promising but requires standardization, validation and scalable formulations. This study reports the development and pre-clinical validation of a standardized poly-herbal nootropic compound (PHNC) for reversal of cognitive frailty. Methods: PHNC was formulated by standardised extracts of Bacopa monnieri (45% bacosides, 200mg), Withania somnifera (5% withanolides, 150mg), Centella asiatica (40% asiaticosides, 150mg), Convolvulus pluricaulis (20% convolvine, 100mg) and Ginkgo biloba (24% flavone glycosides, 60 mg) using piperine (5mg) as bioenhancer. Standardisation, quantification and characterization of marker compounds using HPLC fingerprinting was followed by scale-up optimization using QbD (Quality by Design) approach to measure granule flow and stability. In-vitro assays for anti-IL-6, AChE inhibition, antioxidant activity and neuroprotection (SH-SY5Y cells) were performed. Standardisation and blind comparability testing was performed by validation laboratories. The 150mg/kg D-galactose+ LPS rat model (in silico AI) was used to induce aged cognitive frailty. 18-month equivalent aged rats were given PHNC at 100, 200, 400 mg/kg, donepezil 3 mg/kg or vehicle for 60 days, followed by evaluation of cognition and neurochemistry. Morris Water Maze, Y-maze and Novel Object Recognition test was used to evaluate cognition, while brain homogenate levels of neurochemical, neuroinflammatory, and oxidative markers were evaluated (Western Blot). Brain histology for CA1/CA3 regions of hippocampus was performed. Results: PHNC showed excellent batch-to-batch reproducibility (marker recovery>95%), flow characteristics (Carr's index 14.2%) and stability (12 months accelerated conditions). In-vitro, PHNC inhibited AChE (IC50 42.3 g/mL), exhibited potent antioxidant activity (DPPH inhibition IC50 28.6 g/mL), and significantly (p<0.001) inhibited IL-6 release (71%) from LPS treated BV2 microglial cells. In the aged rat model by in silico AI, PHNC (400mg/kg) significantly improved cognition, reducing escape latency in MWM (from 68.4s to 24.1s), boosting recognition index (72.8% vs frail control 41.2%, p<0.001), with effects comparable to donepezil. Brain levels of BDNF increased (2.8-fold), hippocampal AChE activity reduced (54%), TNF- and IL-1 reduced (64% and 58%, respectively) along with GSH restoration and neuronal counts in hippocampus. No toxicity was observed at 2000mg/kg. Conclusion: PHNC is a standardized medicinal plant derived nootropic formulation that improves cognition through multi-pathway modulation, including improving cholinergic activity, BDNF levels and dampening neuroinflammation, with QbD-based scalable manufacturing for clinical validation.
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Shibanjan Paul Roy

title: Editorial: Identification of neurological biomarkers for neurodegenerative disorders
abstract: A neurodegenerative disease can be marked by distinct biological, cognitive, and behavioral changes. While traditional diagnostic frameworks, acting as late-stage detection systems, rely on the exploration of behavioral symptoms and cognitive profiling, biological markers matter because they bridge the gap between the initiation of irreversible structural damage and the onset of observable symptoms, a gap that behavioral and cognitive assessments structurally cannot address.Disease-modifying therapies only work before overt symptoms begin, the exact phase where clinical diagnosis currently fails. To address these emerging challenges, this research topic brings together studies that advance biomarker discovery and clinical translation across neurodegenerative disorders. This collection comprises 13 articles, including six original research articles, two systematic reviews, two reviews, two mini reviews and one brief research report. The articles focus on current approaches to the biomarker discovery and its implications in neurodegenerative disorders. 2026) compared retinal and optic nerve head microvasculature using OCT-A in asymptomatic HTLV-1 carriers and HAM/TSP patients. Although no significant differences emerged, reduced peripapillary flux index in HAM/TSP suggested its potential as a biomarker of disease progression warranting further investigation. The study by Renga et al. (2026) used multimodal MRI to compare ALS patients with healthy controls, revealing widespread network disruption and altered structural-functional coupling. These findings support ALS as a network-level neurodegenerative disorder and highlight multimodal connectomic measures as potential biomarkers. Xu et.al. (2026), investigated if the combined triglyceride glucose (TyG) and non high density lipoprotein cholesterol (non-HDL-C) could predict early cognitive impairment following acute ischemic stroke. It was also found that higher TyG and non-HDL-C levels were independently associated with an increased post-stroke cognitive impairment, with their combined use improving predictive accuracy. Santacesaria et al. (2026) found that patients with Parkinson's disorder (PD) without mild cognitive impairment (MCI) showed normal prospective memory performance despite distinct oscillatory patterns, suggesting compensatory neural mechanisms. Time-based prospective memory involved increased alpha, theta, and beta power, whereas event-based memory showed reduced power, indicating differing attention-control strategies despite preserved performance.The study by Chen et.al. (2025), found that a higher MRI derived global cerebral small vessel disease burden is associated with hippocampal sclerosis, higher is the cognitive impairment, and more advanced stages along the Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum, suggesting it may serve as a useful imaging biomarker for AD. The study on multiple sclerosis atrophy (MSA) by Huang et.al. (2025) found that low baseline serum total cholesterol independently predicted higher mortality, indicating serum cholesterol may serve as a prognostic biomarker for survival in MSA.The meta analysis by You et.al. (2026), found that a higher neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is linked to the presence and higher burden on cerebral small vessel disease, especially the ischemic markers. This suggests that NLR may serve as inflammatory biomarkers for ischemic cerebral small vessel disease, requiring further investigation through longitudinal studies. The review article by Altuna (2026) examines the shift in early cognitive screening following the introduction of disease-modifying therapies for Alzheimer's disease. While traditional paper tools remain practical, they lack sensitivity and are prone to biases. Digital cognitive phenotyping offers an accessible approach to stratifying early risk guiding further testing and diagnosis.The systematic review by Yang et. al. (2026) evaluates the use and predictive value of Galectin-3 as a blood biomarker for early cognitive development. Elevated peripheral Gal-3 was associated with cognitive impairment. The authors concluded that Gal-3 can be an accessible and non-invasive biomarker for the early detection of vascular-related cognitive decline and MCl, however, its further role in AD is yet to be clarified. Guo et. al. (2025) focuses on the shift towards multimodal biomarkers; neuroimaging, blood/CSF proteins, genetics, digital tracking and clinical tests; for early detection of MCI in PD. AI use can overcome the low sensitivity of traditional paper tests to enable precise risk understanding and timely interventions to delay progression to dementia. Li et. al. ( 2025) highlights the dual nature of Interleukin-6, a cytokine that acts as a pro-inflammatory agent in the brain and a beneficial myokine that promotes neuroplasticity. Chronic inflammation elevates harmful IL-6-trans-signalling, whereas exercise typically triggers the classical IL-6 signaling pathways that support neuroprotective factors. Getahun et. al. (2025) found that declining retinal total macular volume (TMV) in 11 RVCL-S patients over two years was associated with worsening brain pathology. Using OCT and MRI, the study suggests retinal TMV may serve as an accessible biomarker for monitoring cerebral disease progression. Deng et al. (2025) found that CSF p-tau217 had the highest standalone diagnostic accuracy for Alzheimer's disease (95% sensitivity, 94% specificity). The Aβ42/p-tau181 ratio showed the best combined performance, supporting a panel of p-tau217 and Aβ42/p-tau181 for early AD diagnosis.Through these research papers, what seems to be clear is that clinical diagnosis of neurodegeneration must adopt a multimodal structure, integrating biological markers in addition to traditional behavioral and cognitive metrics. With the advent of artificial intelligence, clinicians must integrate AI platforms to assist clinical judgement, in order to enable personalized and comprehensive diagnosis immune to the risks of traditional assessment methods.Despite the recent advancements in understanding the biomarkers of neurodegenerative disorders, significant challenges remain. Most of the studies, especially the neuroimaging and EEG study, are limited by the small sample size. High cost and limited accessibility to the advanced technologies required to identify the biomarkers further hinder the progress of research. In addition, global standardisation and validation of the studies of the biomarkers becomes difficult due to the aforementioned factors.Future research should address the existing limitations and enhance the clinical implications of biomarkers. Multimodal biomarkers could improve diagnosis and prognosis, while cost effective wearable technologies could collect digital biomarkers. In addition, developing deep learning and artificial intelligence models could integrate the biomarkers and predict the predisposition to neurodegenerative disorders.This collection aims at understanding recent advances in aforementioned areas, contributing significantly to the field of biomarkers in order to make clinical diagnosis of neurodegeneration more holistic, accurate and biologically informed.
authors: K. Jayasankara Reddy, Sruthy Nair

title: Altered stimulus-specific adaptation at the auditory cortex of a mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome
abstract: Abstract Auditory hypersensitivity or decreased sound tolerance is a common phenotype of Fragile X Syndrome (FXS). Impairments in adaptation, defined as the reduction in the neuronal responsiveness to repeating sounds, can contribute to this prevalent phenotype. Previous studies on event-related potential observed impairments in mismatch negativity (MMN) in both FXS individuals and in the FMR1 -knockout (KO) mouse model of FXS. Therefore, in the present study we characterized stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA), a neural correlate of MMN, at the auditory cortex (AC) of anesthetized (with ketamine/xylazine) female and male postnatal day 20 (P20) wild-type (WT) and FMR1 -KO mice, using the oddball paradigm with either 4 Hz or 1 Hz repetition rate. We observed robust SSA at the 4 Hz repetition rate of the oddball paradigm in the AC neurons of all four groups of animals. We also noted that the strength of SSA diminished between 4 to 1 Hz repetition rate. In addition, at both the 4 Hz and 1 Hz repetition rate, reduced SSA was observed particularly in the male FMR1 -KO mice compared to their WT counterparts, while female WT and FMR1 -KO mice displayed similar SSA. In terms of sex differences, male FMR1 -KO mice had lower SSA than female FMR1 -KO mice, while SSA was similar in male and female WT mice. Overall, our observation of reduced SSA in the male FMR1 -KO mice suggests that impairments in neuronal adaptation potentially contribute to the auditory hypersensitivity phenotype particularly within the male population.
authors: Abdullah Abdullah, Xiuping Liu, Jun Yan, Ning Cheng

title: Title: Gene expression, neuroinflammation, and neural plasticity in type 2 diabetes: Translational insights from exercise and cognitive modulation
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) increases vulnerability to cognitive decline through interacting disturbances in insulin signaling, mitochondrial energetics, redox and lipid homeostasis, neuroimmune regulation, neurovascular coupling, and experience-dependent plasticity. This review integrates molecular, cellular, preclinical, and clinical evidence linking these processes to altered gene expression, glial dysfunction, synaptic instability, and impaired cognition. We distinguish well-supported mechanisms from unresolved questions concerning causality, cell-type specificity, human hippocampal remodeling, context-dependent pharmacological effects, and the translational limitations of experimental models. On this basis, we propose an integrative framework in which metabolic flexibility acts as a permissive gatekeeper for neural adaptation. AMPK-centered signaling supports mitochondrial quality control, autophagy, antioxidant defenses, and restraint of NF-kB/NLRP3-associated inflammation, but is considered necessary rather than sufficient for cognitive recovery. Durable plasticity additionally requires activity-dependent CREB-BDNF signaling and adequate neurovascular support to match energy delivery with circuit demand. Exercise, cognitive training, environmental enrichment, metformin, and incretin-based therapies engage complementary components of this network, although their efficacy is likely to vary with age, metabolic state, inflammatory burden, vascular reserve, treatment timing, and adherence. The framework predicts that metabolic activation without circuit engagement will provide limited cognitive benefit, whereas plasticity-promoting interventions will be constrained by persistent metabolic or vascular dysfunction. We therefore argue for multimodal, biomarker-informed strategies that integrate metabolic stabilization, vascular support, and structured physical and cognitive stimulation. Long-term randomized studies combining neuroimaging with molecular and metabolic profiling are required to test these predictions and define precision approaches for preserving cognitive resilience in T2DM.
authors: Cristovam Guerreiro Diniz, Natáli Valím Oliver Bento-Torres, Emanuel Ramos da Costa, Nara Gyzely de Morais Magalhães, Mauro André Damasceno de Melo et al.

title: Melatonin attenuates ferroptosis-associated injury through modulation of the thioredoxin-interacting protein/thioredoxin-1/glutathione peroxidase 4 pathway after neonatal hypoxic ischemic brain damage
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to elucidate the neuroprotective mechanism of melatonin (Mel) against hypoxic-ischemic brain damage (HIBD) in neonatal rats, specifically through the thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP)/thioredoxin-1 (Trx-1)/glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) pathway in neuronal ferroptosis, and to concurrently evaluate its therapeutic efficacy using multimodal MRI. METHODS: A neonatal rat HIBD model was established with pre- and postmodeling Mel administration. Neuroprotective effects were dynamically assessed in vivo via multimodal MRI. Hippocampal tissues were analyzed for ferroptosis markers and pathway components. In vitro , PC12 cells underwent oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) with or without Mel. TXNIP-overexpressing cells were used to verify the axis's specific role. RESULTS: MRI confirmed that Mel significantly reduced infarct volume and improved cerebral blood flow (all P < 0.05). It preserved neuronal and mitochondrial integrity. Molecularly, Mel restored GPX4/Trx-1 and suppressed acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4/TXNIP (all P < 0.05). These effects were replicated in OGD-PC12 cells and persisted in TXNIP-overexpressing cells, supporting the involvement of this pathway. CONCLUSION: Mel attenuates acute neonatal HIBD and reduces ferroptosis-associated neuronal injury, potentially involving modulation of the TXNIP/Trx-1/GPX4 pathway. Multimodal MRI may serve as a useful in-vivo tool for evaluating therapeutic responses after neonatal HIBD.
authors: Youcheng Qin, Peilun Xiao, Xinyue Zhang, Zhigang Yang, Wenjie Xiang et al.

title: Biomechanical Analysis of Traumatic Brain Injury Based on Non-human Primate Model
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a common and severe injury in aerospace, transportation, sports, and military scenarios. Establishing reliable TBI simulation models and injury assessment systems is essential for determining TBI tolerance thresholds and developing protection criteria. Due to ethical constraints on human impact experiments, non-human primates (NHP) offer translational advantages owing to their close similarities to humans in gyrencephalic brain morphology, functional connectivity, and genomic composition. This review systematically analyzes the research progress of methods involved in: (1) NHP-based TBI simulation models, encompassing physical impact models, finite element models, and (2) NHP-based TBI multi-dimensional injury assessment, covering histopathology, biomarkers, multimodal MRI, neurobehavioral assessments, and biomechanical responses. Given that conventional physical impact models typically employ head-only impact and fail to capture whole-body loading and polytrauma as they usually occur in real-world scenarios, future efforts should focus on developing novel injury models that incorporate such conditions; To improve the biofidelity and predictive accuracy of finite element models, future work should include sulcal-gyral and vascular structures and conduct new impact experiments for model validation; Considering the complexity of TBI manifestations, future studies should establish multi-dimensional assessment databases and introduce machine learning approaches for multi-dimensional injury weight analysis. Collectively, these endeavor would enable a comprehensive understanding of TBI mechanisms and thus guide protective equipment design, thereby enhancing occupant protection in real-world scenarios.
journal: Medicine in Novel Technology and Devices
authors: Yanxian Yue, Qiao Li, Weiping Bu, Xiaopeng Liu, Lizhen Wang et al.

title: Neuroplastic mechanisms of chronic pain: Implications and future directions
abstract: Chronic pain is now increasingly viewed as aberrant neuroplasticity rather than a protracted expression of peripheral nociception. This review integrates current knowledge through the lens of a peripheral-to-central paradigm, whereby peripheral sensory sensitization contributes to pain initiation, spinal excitation–inhibition imbalance and glianeuron signaling amplify and sustain central sensitization, and supraspinal corticolimbic and reward-network remodeling contributes to persistent pain as well as affective or cognitive comorbidities. Across neuropathic, inflammatory, osteoarthritis-related, pelvic, postoperative, visceral, and diabetic pain, higher-level processes show broad cross-disorder convergence, whereas the dominant molecular mediators, immune-cell populations, and circuit mechanisms frequently remain disease- and model-specific. The strongest mechanistic evidence comes from animal studies, while neuroimaging, behavioral phenotyping, and molecular markers are complementary but not yet clinically validated measures of pain-related plasticity. Pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions have shown preclinical potential for modulating these mechanisms, although evidence for mechanism-guided precision treatment remains limited. Future studies need to implement longitudinal, sex-inclusive, and cross-model designs that integrate cell-specific manipulation, multimodal imaging, multi-omics, and prospective clinical validation in order to differentiate causal drivers from secondary adaptations and translate knowledge of neuroplastic mechanisms into clinically actionable strategies.
authors: Kaikai Wang, Yanhu He, Jinhai Liu, Shaobai Li, Chengyi Yuan et al.

title: Neurobiological mechanisms and brain network dysfunction in major depressive disorder: an integrative review
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent and disabling psychiatric disorder characterized by persistent mood disturbances, cognitive impairments, and significant systemic consequences. Despite its substantial clinical burden, diagnosis remains challenging because current approaches rely largely on subjective symptom-based assessments and are complicated by marked biological and clinical heterogeneity. In this review, we synthesize findings from neuroimaging, electrophysiology, genetics, and molecular studies to provide an integrated overview of the structural, functional, and neurobiological alterations that underlie MDD. We discuss abnormalities involving large-scale brain networks, neuroplasticity and stress-related pathways, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and neurotransmitter systems, together with their implications for biomarker discovery, patient stratification, and treatment response. Collectively, current evidence implicates both molecular dysregulation and large-scale neural network dysfunction in MDD, although direct evidence linking alterations across these biological levels remains limited. Integrating multimodal biological and neuroimaging approaches may improve diagnostic precision, facilitate personalized therapeutic strategies, and advance the development of biologically informed psychiatry.
authors: Dina Iskakova, Burcu Yener, Altyngul T. Kamzanova, Aygul Sitakanova, Rifat Hamoudi et al.

title: Attenuation of self-produced touch in the posterior insula reflects body image disturbances in anorexia nervosa
abstract: Abstract Body image disturbance (BID) is a core feature of anorexia nervosa (AN), encompassing multimodal distortions in bodily self-perception. Affective touch, a gentle, emotionally salient tactile stimulus, is implicated in body ownership but has not been extensively studied in AN. Affective touch is processed in the insula, an area involved in interoception and bodily self-awareness which has been shown to be altered both structurally and functionally in AN. This study explored the neural mechanisms underlying BID by examining how individuals with AN process self-produced affective touch. Women with AN ( n = 44) and age-matched healthy controls (HC, n = 40), participated in a self-other-object touch task during functional brain imaging and filled out questionnaires related to body image and eating disorder symptomatology. During self-touch, individuals with AN exhibited increased activation in the right posterior insula compared to object-touch, whereas HC did not. This insular activation correlated positively with body attitude (BAT) and body size estimation (FRS) scores in AN, but negatively in healthy controls, suggesting divergent processing of self-related tactile input. These findings suggest that posterior insular responses to self-produced touch may reflect disturbed sensory self-processing in AN, and that touch-based mechanisms contributing to body ownership in healthy individuals may operate differently in the context of AN. Broadening BID research beyond the visual modality opens new avenues for translational research and treatment.
authors: Morgan Frost-Karlsson, Maria Zetterqvist, Håkan Olausson, Rebecca Boehme

title: Electroencephalography research in neuropathic pain (Review)
abstract: Neuropathic pain (NP), arising from lesions or dysfunction of the somatosensory system, remains a major clinical challenge due to its subjective and multidimensional nature.Traditional pain assessments rely on self-report scales, which lack objectivity and reproducibility.Electroencephalography (EEG), with its high temporal resolution and accessibility, provides a promising avenue for identifying candidate neurophysiological biomarkers of pain.The current narrative review integrates mechanistic insights and electrophysiological evidence to delineate EEG alterations in NP.Resting-state θ increases and dominant-frequency slowing are relatively recurrent in chronic NP, whereas α-, β-and γ-band findings remain heterogeneous.Network analyses further reveal aberrant prefrontal-limbic and sensorimotor connectivity, as well as altered cross-frequency coupling, but the direction and topology of these findings remain dependent on the patient population, recording configuration and analytical metric.Advances in computational EEG analysis, graph theory and machine learning are facilitating exploration of objective, individualized pain assessment frameworks.Emerging portable EEG and multimodal approaches may provide opportunities for future clinical translation.Overall, EEG offers a feasible and dynamic method to bridge subjective pain perception with measurable neurophysiological signatures, paving the way toward precision diagnostics and neuromodulation in NP.Contents 1. Introduction 2. Mechanisms of NP 3. Overall status of EEG in pain research 4. Characteristics of pain-related EEG frequency bands 5. Network connectivity and cross-frequency coupling 6. EEG and electrophysiological changes following central neuromodulation for pain 7. Objective EEG assessment technology route 8. EEG-based assessment of nociception in comatose and non-communicative patients 9. Clinical transformation and decision support 10. Challenges and future directions
authors: Lanling Zhou, Nianshun Liao, Hongmei Wang, Jiaxi Zhao, Haijun Jiang et al.

title: Mixture-of-Experts Electroencephalography-Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Fusion for Interpretable Computer-Assisted Brain Disorder Diagnosis
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provide complementary information about brain function, and have shown significant promise in detecting functional abnormalities in various brain disorders. However, the distinct signal characteristics and disparate representational spaces of EEG and fMRI pose severe challenges to effective multimodal fusion, thereby hindering accurate computer-assisted diagnosis of brain disorders with conventional fixed models. This study presents Brain Mixture-of-Experts (BrainMoE), an adaptive and interpretable EEG-fMRI fusion framework for computer-assisted diagnosis of brain disorders, integrating multimodal brain features through modality-specific experts, a shared neural-state expert, and an adaptive routing mechanism. BrainMoE first projects EEG and fMRI signals into a unified Desikan-Killiany (DK) atlas region-of-interest (ROI) space, then uses graph encoders to extract modality-specific brain-network representations. The soft-routing module produces a routing representation, and the Expert Gate in the Fuse Module generates sample-specific weights to combine the EEG, fMRI, and shared neural-state expert representations. To handle incomplete acquisition scenarios, modality-state masks and missing-modality tokens are incorporated, allowing the same trained model to perform full EEG-fMRI, EEG-only, and fMRI-only inference. Finally, node-occlusion analysis provides ROI-level attribution maps for both EEG- and fMRI-derived predictions. The framework was evaluated on the Healthy Brain Network (HBN) dataset across five binary brain disorder classification tasks, including major depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, reading impairment, autism spectrum disorder, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. BrainMoE outperformed state-of-the-art comparison algorithms, achieving an average AUC of 86.9 ± 3.0%, and ablation experiments supported the contribution of the routing and expert-fusion components. Furthermore, the interpretability analysis identifies group-level ROI contributions to disease classification that are consistent with previously reported neuroimaging findings. This method supports computer-assisted diagnosis of brain disorders by addressing the challenge of integrating heterogeneous EEG-fMRI neural representations while maintaining interpretability and inference under simulated missing-modality conditions.
authors: Ruizhe Zhong, Haisheng Li, Qingchuan Zhang

title: Beyond morphology: A review of heterogeneous mechanisms and precision risk management in left ventricular non-compaction/left ventricular hypertrabeculation
abstract: Left ventricular non-compaction/left ventricular hypertrabeculation (LVNC/LVHT) has traditionally been regarded as a congenital cardiomyopathy caused by arrested myocardial compaction during embryogenesis. However, this classical concept is increasingly challenged by mounting clinical and basic evidence, in view of its marked heterogeneity in clinical presentation, imaging features, and genetic background. This review systematically synthesizes relevant research from recent years to propose that LVNC/LVHT is better understood not as a single discrete disease entity, but as a morphological endpoint resulting from diverse etiologies and mechanisms. This review critically appraises the phenotypic pitfalls of current imaging diagnostic criteria, highlighting the clinical dilemma of concurrent over-diagnosis and under-diagnosis that leads to inappropriate management. It then delineates two distinct pathogenic pathways: A developmental pathway associated with mutations in genes such as TAZ and MYH7 and dysregulation of signaling pathways including transforming growth factor-β and neuregulin 1–erythroblastic leukemia viral oncogene homolog; and an acquired/adaptive pathway linked to hemodynamic load-induced myocardial remodeling. Based on these insights, we propose an integrated classification framework subdividing LVNC/LVHT into development-driven, load-adaptive, and idiopathic benign trabeculation subtypes to resolve long-standing diagnostic confusion. We further introduce a multimodal risk stratification system incorporating cardiac structure and function, electrophysiology, genetics, circulating biomarkers, and systemic factors. This strategy aims to shift LVNC/LVHT management from a morphology-based, one-size-fits-all paradigm toward mechanism-guided, individualized precision care. Finally, we outline future directions, including validation of risk models, mechanistic studies, updated guidelines, and integration of artificial intelligence and multi-omics, to establish a novel precision diagnostic and therapeutic framework for LVNC/LVHT.
authors: Changying Zhao, Ran Ran, Shiquan Sun, Tao Shi, Yang Yan et al.

title: A hierarchical framework for nociplastic pain mechanisms
abstract: Nociplastic pain refers to pain arising from altered nociceptive processing in the absence of tissue damage or somatosensory system lesion sufficient to explain the symptoms. Despite the high prevalence and clinical burden of conditions characterized by nociplastic pain, current treatment strategies remain only partially effective, partly because the mechanisms sustaining nociplastic pain are heterogeneous and incompletely defined. Central sensitization remains an important neurophysiological construct, particularly when used to describe activity-dependent amplification of nociceptive processing, but it should not be treated as a complete explanation for pain persistence and heterogeneity. Here, we propose a hierarchical framework in which nociplastic pain mechanisms are conceptualized as interacting processes spanning spinal gain amplification, brainstem descending modulation, thalamocortical sensory gating, intrinsic network integration, corticolimbic affective-motivational processing, and perceptual inference. Neuroimmune signaling is considered a putative cross-level modulator of excitability and plasticity. The framework also illustrates how non-selective pharmacological perturbations could be used to test selected model components in prospective biomarker-defined studies. The framework generates falsifiable predictions linking pre-treatment sensory, neurophysiological, neuroimaging, molecular, affective, and behavioral profiles to treatment response and functional recovery. Overall, this review proposes a mechanism-informed structure for patient stratification and for the future design of multimodal interventions targeting specific contributors to nociplastic pain rather than relying on diagnostic labels or single-mechanism explanations alone.
authors: Panos Zanos, Andria Michael, Neofyta Faidonos, Charalambos Papacharalambous

title: Electrophysiological and computational analysis of burst generation in Drosophila class III cold nociceptors
abstract: Introduction In Drosophila larvae, Class III (CIII) primary sensory neurons detect nociceptive cold temperatures, with about half responding to rapid cooling with transient bursting [1,2]. Cold responses have been linked to activation of thermosensitive TRP channels, including TRPM, PKD2, and NOMPC [1,3]. We previously showed that lowering extracellular Cl⁻ enhances spiking and promotes bursting in CIII neurons, consistent with a depolarizing shift of the Cl⁻ reversal potential. Here, we test whether pharmacological or ionic perturbations that produce appropriate membrane depolarization are sufficient to create bursting mechanisms in CIII neurons at room temperature, revealing a mechanism that does not rely on TRP channel activation. Methods Intracellular recordings were obtained from CIII neurons in Drosophila larvae under pharmacological and ionic manipulations. Experimental conditions included reduced extracellular Cl- (6 mM; 134 mM control), elevated extracellular K+ (15 mM; 3 mM control), Ca2+ removal, and tetrodotoxin (TTX, 20 nM) to block voltage-gated Na+ channels. Direct current injection was used to characterize transitions between silence, spiking, and bursting across conditions. In parallel, a biophysical computational model of the CIII neuron was developed and constrained by experimental measurements. Model parameters were tuned to reproduce passive electrical properties and validated by comparison with experimentally observed activity patterns. Results In control, current injection (5–20 pA) produced tonic spiking. In low-Cl⁻ saline, the same stimulation induced bursting in 90% of neurons (18/20). Elevated extracellular K⁺ promoted bursting in all neurons examined (6/6), indicating that global depolarization facilitates burst generation. Removal of extracellular Ca²⁺ did not eliminate bursting, suggesting that Ca²⁺ influx is not strictly required for burst generation under these conditions. In contrast, tetrodotoxin (20 nM) abolished both spikes and the underlying depolarizing potentials. Biophysical modeling reproduced these transitions and suggested that the voltage-gated Na⁺ current plays a prominent role in sustaining the depolarizing envelope supporting burst generation. Discussion These results demonstrate that CIII neurons can generate the full spectrum of activity patterns—silence, tonic spiking, and bursting—without activation of thermosensitive TRP channels. Depolarizing manipulations such as reduced extracellular Cl-, elevated K+, or current injection reliably promoted bursting. These findings suggest that practically all CIII neurons are intrinsically burst-capable when operating within an appropriate depolarized regime. Biophysical modeling reproduced the observed transitions and dissected the contributions of ionic gradients and membrane conductances, providing a mechanistic framework in which Na+ channel dynamics contribute prominently to the generation of bursting activity. Acknowledgments NIH grant R01NS115209 to DNC and GSC. authors: Akira Sakurai, S. М. Коrogod, Daniel N. Cox, Gennady  S. Cymbalyuk

title: MOLECULAR ATLAS OF AGING. META-GROUP 14. COMPLEMENT SYSTEM: TWO-FACED JANUS, PROTECTING AND DESTROYING AT THE SAME TIME. INTEGRATIVE APPROACH IN THE CONTEXT OF THE THEORY OF META-ENVIRONMENTS AND META-REGULATORS
abstract: Relevance. The complement system is a cascade of more than 50 plasma and tissue proteins that provides rapid protection against pathogens, the removal of damaged cells, and the connection between innate and adaptive immunity. In youth, it works as a verified mechanism: it recognizes the foreign, activates the cascade, destroys the threat, and shuts down. However, with age, this mechanism fails. Chronic inflammation (inflamaging) keeps the complement system in a state of constant activation. Levels of key components — C3, C4, C5, C9 — increase. Anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a become chronically elevated. The membrane-attack complex C5b-9 accumulates in tissues. The complement system acquires a Janus two-face: on the one hand, it continues to protect — elevated levels of complement proteins in the elderly can suppress neuroinflammation and autoimmunity; On the other hand, its chronic activation becomes an independent driver of inflammation, destroying blood vessels, brain, kidneys and accelerating all age-related diseases. Aim. To present age-related dysregulation of the complement system as the fourteenth level of molecular aging, the main amplifier that turns local age-related damage into a systemic fire. To substantiate the need for systemic restoration of the regulatory balance of complement through the tuning of meta-regulators. Results. It was shown that systemic complement activation occurs with age: the levels of C1q, C4, C3, C5 and C9, as well as anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a and the soluble membrane attack complex sC5b-9 increase. The level of expression of complement proteins correlates not with chronological age, but with the "actionable-time aging", determining the rate of inflammatory aging. Activation occurs mainly through the classical pathway, which indicates the accumulation of immune complexes. Anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a bind to receptors on a variety of cells, triggering inflammation, chemotaxis, neuronal damage, and inducing a senescent phenotype through epigenetic mechanisms (DNA methylation). The membrane-attacking complex C5b-9 damages the endothelium, neurons, and epithelium. At the same time, the complement system demonstrates a paradoxical two-facedness: its hyperactivation enhances pathologies, but increased complement levels in the elderly can suppress neuroinflammation and autoimmunity. A multimodal approach (the Quatotron method) to the physiological restoration of the regulatory balance of complement through the reduction of systemic inflammation and the restoration of endogenous regulatory mechanisms has been proposed. Conclusion. The complement system is the fourteenth level of molecular aging, the main amplifier that turns local damage into a systemic inflammatory fire. Its systemic recovery through the control of meta-regulators opens up new opportunities for the prevention of age-associated diseases and healthy longevity.
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Лагода

title: Brain network topology and neural mechanisms in Sanda athletes: a comparative study across training levels
abstract: Purpose: This study investigated the topological organization of brain networks in Sanda athletes across different training levels to elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying the sport's exceptional sensorimotor integration and training-related neural plasticity. Methods: Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were collected from 35 participants, including elite athletes, second-level athletes, and novices. Using the Automated Anatomical Labeling 116-region atlas (AAL116), structural connectivity (SC) networks were constructed based on fractional anisotropy (FA) derived from diffusion tensor imaging, while functional connectivity (FC) networks were computed using Pearson correlations between regional blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) time series. Structure-function coupling (SFC) networks were generated as a weighted linear combination of SC and FC. Network differences were assessed using Network-Based Statistic (NBS) and graph-theoretical analyses. Results: Elite athletes exhibited prominent structure-function coupling within visual-motor-executive pathways, whereas novices showed greater involvement of language-rhythm-related pathways. At the global level, elite athletes demonstrated stronger small-world organization and network synchrony, suggesting more efficient information transmission. At the nodal level, the parietal-cerebellar system emerged as a critical hub across the examined networks, with particularly prominent involvement of the right supramarginal gyrus (SMG.R) and right cerebellar lobule VI (CRBL6.R). Discussion: These regions are likely to play a central role in sensorimotor integration and rhythm control. These findings confirm that long-term Sanda training optimizes brain network topology, providing key insights into the neural plasticity of athletic expertise.
authors: Yang Chen, Zifeng Jia, Zhangzhi Zhao, Jihe Zhou, Yuanzheng Lin et al.

title: Brain Network and Synaptic Plasticity Changes Associated with Electroconvulsive Therapy for Depression: A Multilevel Review
abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is an important treatment for severe, treatment-resistant, or high-risk depression, yet the relationship between its antidepressant effects, brain network changes, and cellular and molecular processes remains incompletely understood. Recent advances in multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), molecular biology, and animal electroconvulsive stimulation models have provided multilevel evidence for understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of ECT in depression. Current studies suggest that ECT is accompanied by changes in functional connectivity within large-scale brain networks, including the default mode network (DMN), the frontoparietal control network (FPCN), and prefrontal-limbic circuits. In parallel, processes involving neurotransmission, brain metabolism, neurotrophic factors, inflammatory responses, and synaptic plasticity may provide biological clues for interpreting these network-level changes. This review summarizes evidence related to brain network reorganization and synaptic plasticity-associated regulation in ECT for depression, and discusses how findings across levels may be integrated to inform future mechanistic research and treatment-response prediction.
journal: International Journal of Public Health and Medical Research
authors: Yihan Jiang, Xinying Jiang, Yuting Huang, Xiaohui Yu

title: 256. Improving working memory in mice using pro-cognitive drugs in the trial unique non-matched to location task
abstract: Abstract Background The trial unique non-matched to location (TUNL) task is a touchscreen-based assay of working memory in rodents. While pharmacological impairment is widely used in rats, pharmacological enhancement of performance in rats or mice has not been demonstrated in literature. Aims & Objectives We employed a recently optimized mouse version of the TUNL task to test compounds modulating glutamatergic and cholinergic signaling. Method Performance was assessed across varying cognitive loads, and functional ultrasound imaging was used to probe neural circuit activity. Results The muscarinic antagonist scopolamine impaired performance to chance levels, whereas the glycine transporter 1 inhibitor bitopertin significantly improved accuracy. Both bitopertin and the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil enhanced performance under high cognitive demand, while scopolamine reduced performance even on easier trials. Bitopertin also rescued deficits induced by the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801. Furthermore, functional ultrasound imaging revealed that bitopertin prevented ketamine-induced alterations in cerebral blood volume within prefrontal, hippocampal, and thalamic regions. Discussion & Conclusions These findings establish the mouse TUNL task as a sensitive tool for detecting pharmacological modulation of working memory in both improvements and impairments. Bitopertin and donepezil show promise as cognitive enhancers, with bitopertin additionally counteracting NMDA receptor–mediated impairments.
authors: Bastiaan van der Veen, Tudor M. Ionescu, Serena Deiana, Wiebke Nissen, Carsten Tobias Wotjak et al.

title: 350. Transcriptomic analysis of mouse brain tissue demonstrates similarity between sleep deprivation and neuronal hyperexcitation-induced gene expression
abstract: Abstract Background Sleep deprivation is associated with numerous health problems and has been linked to neuronal hyperexcitation, a potential driver of its neurological harm. Aims & Objectives This study aimed to elucidate the transcriptomic relationship between sleep deprivation and neuronal hyperexcitation. Method To achieve this aim, publicly available gene expression data from acutely sleep-deprived mice and neuronal hyperexcitation model mice were compared using the running Fisher algorithm in the bioinformatics platform BaseSpace. In total 21 bulk-RNA datasets (hippocampus, hypothalamus and cerebellum), 11 scRNA-seq sleep deprivation datasets (hypothalamus and cortex) containing cell population data from neurons, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia, and endothelial cells, and 23 bulk-RNA hippocampal hyperexcitation datasets (models: optogenetics, bicuculline, KCl depolarization, kainite and pilocarpine) were analyzed. The data spanned diverse conditions of sex, age and sampling time. Results The comparative transcriptomic analysis yielded several key findings. The data revealed a significant positive transcriptomic correlation between sleep deprivation and neuronal hyperexcitation models. Neuronal hyperexcitation datasets whose samples were collected within 1-12 hours post seizure induction showed higher correlation with sleep deprivation. Analysis of a bulk-RNA sleep deprivation dataset revealed gene functional groups shared between the two conditions were associated with plasticity, immune response, and inflammation pathways. Among the most commonly overexpressed genes shared by the two conditions were immediate early genes such as Jun, Egr1/2/4, Fos, Bdnf, Arc and Homer1 and injury-associated genes such as Ptgs2 and Ctgf. The scRNA datasets revealed that microglia, neurons, and endothelial cells from sleep-deprived mice are the cell types most closely connected with hyperexcitation. Microglia hyperexcitation-associated genes included stress- and immune-response related genes such as Junb/d, Cebpb and Cd14. Neurons highly expressed immediate early genes such as Jun/d, Fos, H3f3b, Tubb3 and Prkar1b. Endothelial cells showed high expression of metabolism-related genes such as Plat, Ucp2 and Dbp. Discussion & Conclusions The molecular findings provide insight into the potential mechanisms underlying the link between sleep deprivation and neuronal hyperexcitation. Specificially, the higher correlation observed in datasets collected 1-12 hours post seizure induction aligns with the expression patterns of immediate early genes in neuronal hyperexcitation models. Furthermore, the overexpression of injury-related genes such as Ptgs2 and Ctgf suggests potentially toxic levels of excitation. Increased microglial activation, neuronal immediate early gene expression, and upregulation of metabolism related genes are all consistent with hyperexcitation-related molecular changes. These mechanisms may be capable of causing long-term changes in brain activity through microglial mediated-inhibitory synapse pruning, neuronal long-term potentiation facilitated by plasticity-associated immediate early gene overexpression and increased brain angiogenesis linked to Dbp overexpression. Together these findings suggest sustained sleep deprivation could result in long-term increases in brain excitation, potentially exacerbating excitatory/inhibitory imbalances and contributing to the development of neuropsychiatric disorders.
authors: Markos Michail Chatzigiannis, Hideo Hagihara, T Miyakawa

title: 790. How can we protet D-neuron?
abstract: Abstract Background In humans, the D-neuron system in nucleus accumbens (D16), projection field of mesolimbic dopamine (DA) system, is far developed than in other animal species. "D-cell hypothesis of schizophrenia" (Ikemoto K., Lancet, 2025) has shown the lack of D-neurons in the D16 of post-mortem brains of schizophrenia, being the cause of mesolimbic dopamine (DA) hyperactivity and psychostic states, such as paranoid-hallucinatory state, excitement or suicide. An immunohistochemical difficulty in visualization of human D-neurons (TAAR1 ligand neurons, = aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC)-only-immunoreactive neurons) has unexpectedly delayed D-neuron reserach. The majority of pathological autopsy brain samples of schizophrenia used for the previous studies, was limited in chronic or residual state of schizophrenia, died in hospitals. Whereas, legal autopsy brain samples have only few clinical informations. Dysfunction of subventricular and/or hippocampal NSC would cause D-neuron dysfunction. Biochemical studies have shown increased level of serum β-phenylethylamine (β-PEA) in severest stage of manic state or paranoid-hallucinatory state of schizophrenia, and decreased level of β-PEA in chronic phase of both diseases. In former stage, inflammation is supposed to affect on D-neurons. Causative triggers of an acute psychotic state contained stress, abuse, excessive alcohol intake, psychostimulant (methamphetamine) use, trauma, infection, malnutrition, degeneration, and so on, which may cause inflammation and cell death. I had been only one woman psychiatrist in the nearest heart hospital from the 1st Nuclear Power Plant of Fukushima, Iwaki Kyoritsu General Hospital (= Iwaki City Medical Center, Japan) for about 12 years, following the Great East Japan Earthquake and nuclear disaster, and examined more than 500 suicidal attempt inpatients and patients with paranoid-hallucinatory state, introduced from the Emergency Center. Aims & Objectives The aim of the present study is to reveal trigger situations leading to the onset of psychotic states, such as paranoid-hallucinatory state and suicidal attempt, in which D-neuron dysfunction might be involved, and is also to explore how to protect the D16 D-neuron, projection field of mesolimbic DA system. Method I examined medical chart following the Great East Japan Earthquake, of Department of Psychiatry, Iwaki City Medical Center, Japan, retrospectively, focusing on causative triggers of paranoid-hallucinatory state, excitement and suicidal attempt, and referring recent publications available. Results Causative events seemingly trigger paranoid-hallucinatory state and suicidal attempt contained abuse, problems in work places or interpersonal relationships, substance abuse, physical problems etc.. Initial sexual intercourse (without any consent, and/or in extramarital state) or virgin killing was noted to precede depressive state, insomnia, suicidal idea, self-mutilation, and suicide. Clinical history of anxiety disorder, substance abuse, mood disorders (bipolar disorder, depression), post-traumatic stress disorder, or personality disorder was frequently seen among patients with suicidal attempt. Discussion & Conclusions In sound development of the D16 D-neuron, nutrition, exercise, BDNF, immune protection, activaion of subventricular and/or hippocampal NSC, are possibly involved. Drug intoxication, and female sexual abuse of virgin killing may injure D16 D-neurons, and cause sleep disorders. It has been known that incidence of hypnotic use among virgins in population more than 60 years old is less than half. Moral education might serve D16 D-neuron protection, leading to suicide prevention.
authors: Keiko Ikemoto

title: From empirical efficacy to neurovascular and cerebrovascular systems perspective: a bibliometric and visualized analysis of traditional Chinese medicine for vascular dementia
abstract: Objective Vascular dementia (VaD) is a major form of cognitive impairment associated with cerebrovascular injury, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, impaired neurovascular coupling, and progressive disruption of brain homeostasis. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-related interventions for VaD encompass heterogeneous categories, including herbal formulas, single herbs, natural products, plant-derived bioactive compounds, acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and moxibustion. Within this broad landscape, the herbal and natural-product branch provides an important interface linking TCM research with food–medicine homology, neurological nutrition, and neurovascular protection. This bibliometric study aimed to map the research landscape, knowledge structure, hotspots, and emerging trends of TCM-related interventions for VaD, with particular attention to herbal, natural-product, and neurovascular research. Methods English-language articles and reviews related to TCM treatment of VaD published from 1997 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and GraphPad Prism were used to analyze annual publication trends, countries/regions, institutions, authors, journals, co-cited references, and keywords. To address intervention heterogeneity, the findings were interpreted across herbal/natural-product, acupuncture/electroacupuncture, moxibustion, and mixed TCM-related categories. Results A total of 357 publications were included, comprising 256 original articles and 101 reviews. China ranked first with 281 publications and occupied a central position in the collaboration network. High-frequency keywords included “vascular dementia,” “acupuncture,” “cognitive impairment,” “oxidative stress,” “apoptosis,” “hippocampus,” and “chronic cerebral hypoperfusion.” Two major research branches were identified. Herbal formulas, single herbs, natural products, and active compounds were mainly associated with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, autophagy, chronic cerebral hypoperfusion, component characterization, and multi-target regulation. In contrast, acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and moxibustion were more closely related to neuromodulation, hippocampal plasticity, cerebral perfusion, and functional recovery. Emerging topics included network pharmacology, expression profiling, inflammasomes, component characterization, and mixed vascular–neurodegenerative mechanisms. Conclusion The TCM-VaD literature represents a heterogeneous research landscape involving both herbal/natural-product and non-pharmacological intervention branches. Herbal medicines, natural products, and plant-derived bioactive compounds constitute the branch most directly connected with food–medicine homology, neurological nutrition, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory regulation, and neurovascular protection. However, bibliometric attention should not be interpreted as evidence of validated efficacy, and conclusions concerning phytoactive compounds should not be generalized to acupuncture- or moxibustion-related research. Future studies should strengthen intervention stratification, component standardization, mechanistic validation, and clinical translation.
authors: Zixiang Jin, Qiuyue Huang, Xiaofen Jia, Miaomiao Lin, Jingwen Zhao et al.

title: Multi-omic spatial mapping of the human habenula defines the molecular and anatomical organization of medial and lateral subregions
abstract: The habenula (Hb) is a small epithalamic midline structure critical for reward processing and mood regulation that is implicated in many complex brain disorders, including depression and addiction. The molecular anatomy of the Hb has been well-characterized in model organisms, but little is known about its organization in the human brain, including the transcriptomic and epigenetic signatures of spatially-organized lateral (LHb) and medial (MHb) cell types. Here, we generated a high resolution spatiomolecular map of the human Hb using both multiomic single nucleus sequencing (snMultiome) and spatially-resolved transcriptomics. We measured gene expression and chromatin accessibility across 4 MHb and 5 LHb neuronal cell types as defined by transcriptomic conservation with rodents and zebrafish. We identified cell type-specific molecular specializations related to GABAergic and glutamatergic signaling as well as regulatory relationships between open chromatin regions, transcription factors, and target genes associated with depression and addiction. High resolution spatial transcriptomics identified the anatomical location of heterogeneous LHb subpopulations, including two putative inhibitory populations in the LHb. We further characterized cell-type relationships between Hb neurons and glial subtypes and predicted ligand-receptor interactions between LHb and MHb neurons. Finally, we delineated Hb cell types and spatial domains enriched in genes associated with genetic risk for psychiatric disorders, identifying the strongest enrichment in the MHb. Collectively, the generated data and analyses resolve the spatiomolecular organization of the human Hb and identify molecular-genetic associations with neuropsychiatric disease.
authors: Kelsey D. Montgomery, Jonathan M. Werner, Nicholas J. Eagles, Chunyu Liu, Cynthia S. Cardinault et al.

title: Trial-by-Trial Connectivity Reveals Selective Safety-Learning Alterations in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
abstract: : Background Prediction errors (PEs) drive fear learning by signaling discrepancies between expected and actual threat. The amygdala-hippocampus and amygdala-vmPFC circuits are preferentially implicated in threat acquisition and safety learning, but whether PE-related connectivity dynamics are disrupted in PTSD remains unknown. Methods We analyzed fMRI data from 65 participants (21 combat veterans with PTSD, 25 trauma-exposed controls, 19 healthy controls) during a reversal threat conditioning task. Trial-by-trial functional coupling was linked to skin conductance-derived PEs using Bayesian multilevel modeling with group-level interaction terms. Results Amygdala–hippocampus coupling tracked positive PEs in all groups (β = 0.08–0.13, all pd > 99%), with no difference between trauma-exposed groups (Δβ = 0.01, pd = 54.9%, 89% HPDi [-0.07, 0.09]). Amygdala–vmPFC coupling diverged by group: both control groups showed negative coupling–PE associations consistent with safety signaling (combat-exposed: β = −0.08, pd = 99.7%; healthy: β = −0.04, pd = 90.9%), whereas veterans with PTSD showed a reversed association (β = 0.03, pd = 88.9%). The direct contrast between trauma-exposed groups confirmed a robust difference (Δβ = −0.12, pd = 99.6%, 89% HPDi [−0.18, −0.05]). Conclusions PTSD was characterized by altered PE-related amygdala–vmPFC connectivity despite preserved amygdala–hippocampal PE signaling, suggesting a selective disruption of circuitry supporting safety-related updating rather than a generalized deficit in threat learning. The contrasting pattern in trauma-exposed individuals without PTSD may reflect a neural signature of resilience.
authors: Nachshon Korem, Tobias R. Spiller, Ziv Ben‐Zion, Daniela Schiller, Ilan Harpaz‐Rotem et al.

title: Global Developmental Delay and Epilepsy Associated with Variants of Uncertain Significance in ALDH18A1 and GABRG2 : A Case Report
abstract: Global developmental delay (GDD) with epilepsy represents a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders with significant genetic contribution. The increasing use of next-generation sequencing has improved diagnostic evaluation; however, interpretation of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) remains challenging in clinical practice.We report a 2½-year-old female child born of a third-degree consanguineous marriage who presented with global developmental delay, recurrent seizures, hypotonia, proximal muscle weakness, and microcephaly. Developmental delay was noted since infancy, with delayed motor and speech milestones. Seizure onset occurred at 9 months of age in the form of febrile tonic seizures, later progressing to generalized tonic-clonic and reflex anoxic seizures. Neurological examination revealed generalized hypotonia and immature pincer grasp. MRI brain demonstrated shallow sulci, mild cerebral atrophy, thinning of the corpus callosum, and reduced hippocampal volume. Whole exome and mitochondrial genome sequencing identified a homozygous missense variant in ALDH18A1 [c.2233A>G; p.Arg745Gly] and two heterozygous missense variants in GABRG2 [c.644G>A; p.Arg215His and c.1357G>T; p.Ala453Ser], all classified as variants of uncertain significance according to ACMG criteria.The identified genes are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by developmental delay, hypotonia, and epilepsy. Although the detected variants have not been previously reported, significant genotypephenotype overlap suggests possible clinical relevance.This case highlights the complexity of interpreting VUS in paediatric neurogenetics and emphasizes the importance of clinical correlation, parental segregation analysis, and long-term genomic re-evaluation in children with developmental delay and epilepsy.
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Indian Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics (Official Journal of IAP Chapter of Neurodevelopmental Pediatrics)

title: Disentangling the role of cholesterol in tauopathies
abstract: Lipid dysregulation, particularly altered cholesterol metabolism, has been increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative disorders including tauopathies. Tauopathies such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) are characterized by abnormal accumulation of phosphorylated Tau (pTau), driving progressive neuronal dysfunction and cognitive decline. However, the mechanistic link between cholesterol dyshomeostasis and Tau pathology remains incompletely understood. This thesis aimed to explore the relationship between cholesterol metabolism and Tau to advance understanding of disease etiology and inform therapeutic strategies, first examining how Tau pathology alters lipid metabolism, then investigating how early cholesterol disturbances downstream of AD-associated risk genes may contribute to pTau accumulation. Chapter 2 explored how the FTLD-causing MAPT P301S mutation alters brain lipid metabolism in vivo, showing increases in diglycerides, glycosphingolipids, and phosphatidylethanolamine in the hippocampus, alongside reductions in monounsaturated triglycerides. Although pTau accumulation varied widely among Tau transgenic mice of the same age, mice with higher pTau levels also exhibited increased storage lipids (triglycerides and cholesteryl esters), decreased cholesterol synthesis, and reduced 24S-hydroxycholesterol. These findings revealed that MAPT mutations and pTau accumulation each drive distinct changes in the brain lipidome. Building on this, Chapter 3 evaluated the therapeutic potential of pharmacologically enhancing brain cholesterol efflux via CYP46A1-mediated conversion to 24S-hydroxycholesterol, using low-dose efavirenz, an agonist of this enzyme. We found no clear evidence that efavirenz altered pTau or lipid metabolism in two tauopathy mouse models (MAPT P301S and P301S/ApoE4), as high within-group variability prevented reliable assessment. To better predict cell type-specific effects, we treated human iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, and microglia with efavirenz or 24S-hydroxycholesterol. Efavirenz selectively altered several phospholipid and sphingolipid classes, leaving triglycerides and cholesteryl esters unaffected across cell types. 24S-hydroxycholesterol induced a major metabolic shift in neurons and astrocytes, increasing cholesteryl ester accumulation, elevating ABCA1 expression, and downregulating cholesterol biosynthesis genes. Both compounds showed trends toward decreased pTau in neurons. Our in vitro results indicated that efavirenz and 24S-hydroxycholesterol can lead to strong effects on brain-cell lipidomes. However, additional in vivo studies in disease models are required to capture potential changes in cholesterol and overall lipid metabolism following efavirenz treatment. Finally, Chapter 4 investigated how neuronal cholesterol metabolism affects pTau using iPSC-derived neurons modeling APOE3 and APOE4 homozygosity. Through pharmacological and genetic interventions, we demonstrated that mevalonate-cholesterol pathway activity acts as an upstream regulator of pTau, and that the APOE4 genotype can lead to increased neuronal de novo sterol synthesis and pTau levels, albeit in a donor-specific manner. Together, these studies underline a bidirectional interplay between Tau biology and cholesterol homeostasis: the mevalonate-cholesterol pathway regulates pTau, with increased activity driving pTau accumulation, while pTau buildup in turn reduces cholesterol synthesis and 24S-hydroxycholesterol production, and increases storage of cholesterol and fatty acids as neutral lipids.
authors: Almudena Maroto Juanes

title: Gm26550 Modulates Learning and Memory by Increasing IGF1 mRNA Expression and Stability in Nrf2 −/− Mice
abstract: ABSTRACT Nrf2 dysfunction is implicated in learning and memory deficits, but the involvement of non‐coding RNAs in Nrf2‐dependent cognitive regulation remains largely unexplored. Here, by analyzing the expression profiles of lncRNAs and mRNAs in the hippocampus of wild‐type (WT) and Nrf2 knockout (Nrf2 −/− ) mice, we identified a decreased expression of lncRNA Gm26550 in Nrf2 −/− mice. Overexpression of Gm26550 enhances hippocampal neuronal synaptic plasticity and rescues learning and memory deficits in Nrf2 −/− mice. Mechanistically, Nrf2 directly binds the promoter of Gm26550 to drive its transcriptional activation and upregulate its expression. Gm26550 elevates IGF1 abundance via two regulatory pathways to maintain cognitive function: first, it functionally counteracts miR‐26a‐5p‐mediated repression of IGF1; second, it interacts with the KH3/KH4 domain of KHSRP to block KHSRP‐triggered degradation of IGF1 mRNA. Collectively, our results reveal that Gm26550 maintains IGF1 expression and transcript stability through miR‐dependent antagonism and RBP sequestration, thereby governing learning and memory downstream of Nrf2. This work expands the understanding of the downstream molecular network controlled by Nrf2.
authors: Hongfang Wang, Ziyao Wang, Dongyue Zuo, Zhaowen Su, Bowen Song et al.

title: Intact spatial learning in Fmr1–/y, Syngap1+/–, and Grin2b+/– rat models of neurodevelopmental disorders
