authors: Xiaoqin Wang, Bin Lei, Yao Zhou, Foyang Fan, Liang Huang et al.

title: The challenges of magnetic resonance imaging and the promise of portable neurotechnology for advancing scientific discovery about neurodevelopmental disorders
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are conditions that impact cognition, behavior, social, and motor development and have their onset in the "developmental period" (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). This diverse group of conditions includes diagnoses characterized by a range of challenges -from focal limitations in one domain of functioning (e.g., Speech Sound Disorder) to global limitations in intellectual and adaptive functioning (e.g., Intellectual Disability). Given that NDDs are first evident in infancy and early childhood, developmental scientists have emphasized the importance of studying these conditions from the earliest point possible so that effective interventions can be developed to promote optimal outcomes (Masten and Cicchetti, 2010).However, this scientific ideal is not without its challenges, as studying cognition, behavior, and neural functioning in infants and young children, particularly those with atypical cognition and behavior, requires special approaches to ensure that research findings are valid. This is particularly challenging when studying neural functioning, as the demands of some neuroimaging approaches (e.g., magnetic resonance imaging) can exceed the developmental capabilities of the individuals who are the focus of the scientific investigation. This is a barrier to research for NDDs and likely impacts the field's ability to discover the mechanisms driving atypical brain and cognitive development.In this Opinion piece, challenges using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and other neuroimaging tools embedded in healthcare settings (e.g., magnetoencephalography) with individuals with NDDs will be described and the dearth of functional MRI research in one group, children with Down syndrome, will be highlighted. Then recommendations for future research will be put forth, with an emphasis on the utility of portable neurotechnology. Finally, recommendations will be made for neuroimaging studies of NDDs.As healthcare tools, neuroimaging approaches such as MRI, were developed within the medical model of illness, in which a healthcare provider directs care and patients are expected to comply with provider directives (Kumar and Chattu, 2018). In this model, the patient needs to adapt to the medical environment, rather than the medical environment adapting to the patient. Neuroimaging research that uses tools like MRI is also embedded in the medical model, and this presents barriers to research participation for groups with NDDs, as will be described next.Participation in neuroimaging studies conducted in healthcare settings presents many barriers to individuals with NDDs even before the neuroimaging procedures are commenced. Examples include (a) traveling to the medical/research facility, (b) traversing complex, overstimulating environments, (c) waiting for care, and (d) communicating with care providers. These tasks and others have been cited as barriers to healthcare and research participation by individuals with NDDs and their families (Haas et al., 2016;Stein Duker et al., 2022). Once these steps are completed, individuals with NDDs and their families face unique challenges inherent to neuroimaging procedures, like MRI. For example, participants need to (a) lie still with little head motion, (b) tolerate being in an unfamiliar, confined space, and (c) cope with the sensations (noises; vibrations) associated with MRI machines (Greene et al., 2016). These challenges likely contribute to lower research participation for individuals with intellectual limitations, as described next.Among groups with NDDs, such as autism spectrum disorder, there is evidence that intellectual level impacts inclusion in neuroimaging research. For example, Jack and Pelphrey (2017) queried the National Database for Autism Research (NDAR, which is now housed under the larger NIMH National Data Archive) to identify the proportion of neuroimaging studies that focused on different subgroups of autistic individuals. They found that fewer than 1% of studies included people with both verbal and performance IQs that were 1 or more standard deviations below the population mean. This is in spite of the fact that close to 40% of autistic children have intellectual disability (ID; (Shaw, 2025)) which is characterized by intellectual ability levels ~2 or more SDs below the population mean (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).Consistent with these findings, research conducted on Down syndrome, the most common genetic cause of ID (Antonarakis, 2017), has documented lower success rates for MRI acquisition for those with lower IQs. Specifically, Lee et al. (2016) reported a trend for a lower average IQ among participants who could not complete MRI scanning procedures (IQ=49) relative to those who could (IQ=58). In addition, age was significantly associated with scanning success in Lee et al. (2016). Participants who were not able to provide usable MRI data were younger on average, suggesting that developmental level (as approximated by chronological age in this study) also relates to the ability to complete MRI procedures.The challenges collecting useable MRI data from groups with NDDs are likely to be magnified when functional (as opposed to structural) MRI is considered. During structural MRI data acquisition, participants are able to watch a movie or sleep. In contrast, during functional MRI (fMRI) data acquisition, participants either need to be (a) awake but without external stimulation like a movie (i.e., for resting state functional MRI; rsfMRI) or (b) completing a task while MRI data are acquired (i.e., for task-based fMRI).To query how MRI parameters (rsfMRI vs. task-based fMRI vs. other) relate to (a) the quantity of published studies and (b) the age of the participants, a Web of Science literature search was completed focused on Down syndrome (DS), as a case example. The following search terms were used: Title = "Down* syndrome" and Abstract= MRI or "magnetic resonance imaging." A total of 198 published articles were identified. Among these, 83 abstracts were deemed relevant in that they described quantitative neuroimaging investigations of infants, children, or adults (as opposed to studies focused on other organs or brain-focused case series, for example).Among the 83 study abstracts reviewed, 14 included fMRI. (This excluded studies employing positron emission tomography or single-photon emission computed tomography only). Of the 14 studies that included fMRI specifically, 4 employed task-based fMRI. With regard to the age of participants, 58 studies included adults only; 12 included adult and child participants; and 13 included children (or children and infants) only. When the 14 fMRI investigations were examined, none included child participants exclusively (though one included mostly child participants). Thus, for DS, few fMRI (particularly task-based fMRI) studies exist, and most focus on adults. This is problematic for scientific discovery about the brain bases of the complex learning difficulties faced by children with DS and highlights the need for scientists to develop approaches to remove barriers associated with MRI, as discussed next.In order to create developmentally informed, mechanistic theories of the neural bases of the cognitive underpinnings of NDDs, alternative neuroimaging approaches, particularly task-based functional neuroimaging approaches, are needed to permit greater participation. One approach to increase participation is to engage children and families in extensive behavioral training to help them gain the skills necessary to participate in neuroimaging studies within a healthcare setting. There are several examples of behavioral protocols that have been developed to improve research participation for these studies, including those for MRI (Nordahl et al., 2016) and magnetoencephalography (Kuschner et al., 2021).Alternatively, the neuroimaging technology can be modified to meet the needs of the participant. Portable neurotechnologies, such as functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and electroencephalography (EEG), are two approaches that have the potential to remove several barriers. Figure 1a presents a summary of some of the barriers neuroimaging approaches, like MRI, present for participants with NDDs. First, the barrier is presented. Then evidence for the relevance of the barrier to participants with NDDs is provided. Finally, a description of how portable neurotechnology may address these barriers is offered.By definition, portable neurotechnologies, which can be brought into a participant's home, can eliminate the first two barriers to participation presented in Figure 1a -travel and completion of procedures in an unfamiliar environment, which can be especially stressful for families of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (Haas et al., 2016;Stein Duker et al., 2022). Portable neurotechnologies, such as fNIRS and EEG, also eliminate aspects of the MRI experience that can be especially problematic for individuals with NDDs, including being required to remain completely still in a confined space and tolerate loud noises. Elimination of these barriers is particularly crucial to increased participation, as individuals with NDDs present with higher rates of anxiety (Zhou et al., 2026) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; (Perera et al., 2022)) and are more likely to experience sensory sensitivities (Tomchek and Dunn, 2007;Isralowitz et al., 2023) than neurotypical peers. Finally, portable neurotechnologies allow the examiner to interact with the participant in an ecologically valid manner. Examiners are able to sit next to or across from the participant and demonstrate how to do a task. This is crucial for easing anxiety, increasing engagement, and reducing the language demands of tasks by permitting demonstration and gestures. This latter component is crucial for people with NDDs who experience high rates of communication difficulties (Filipe et al., 2023) which can serve as barriers to functional MRI studies where the participants are separated from the examiner and must follow oral instructions over a speaker in the MRI scanner. Figure 1b illustrates how fNIRS studies can be completed with participants in their naturalistic environment, highlighting the removal of barriers associated with MRI and other neuroimaging tools embedded in healthcare settings.In this Opinion piece, the barriers associated with MRI research for individuals with NDDs were presented alongside the promise of portable neurotechnologies to reduce barriers. The promise of these approaches must also come with an acknowledgement that no neuroimaging approach is appropriate for all participants. fNIRS, for example, requires participants to tolerate wearing a snug band or cap on their head during task completion; EEG requires participants to tolerate electrode placement and the sensations associated with them. In order to advance research on the neural bases of the cognitive underpinnings of NDDs, there is a need to identify which neuroimaging approaches work well for which participants and which approaches do not. This is essential for the study of NDDs, as these conditions are associated with a great deal of heterogeneity (Beversdorf, 2024), making a one-size-fits-all approach problematic. Transparency about the generalizability and limitations of neuroimaging research findings is of the utmost importance. Thus, the following suggestions are provided for researchers to consider when designing neuroimaging research studies focused on NDDs. First, researchers should consider embedding neuroimaging investigations into broader behavioral phenotyping studies. When advertising for these studies, it should be clear to families that the successful completion of neuroimaging procedures is not necessary for participation. Rather, it is one component of the study and there is no expectation that all participants will complete these procedures. The hope is that this will reduce the impact of family self-exclusion for neuroimaging studies (i.e., families who do not think their child could complete neuroimaging procedures choose not to sign up). Once participants are enrolled, it will be essential that all participants complete behavioral phenotyping procedures so that researchers can carefully characterize the phenotypes of participants who are and are not able to tolerate neuroimaging procedures. Although many studies are following guidelines regarding the documentation of the inclusion and exclusion of participants in neuroimaging research (e.g., (Nichols et al., 2016)), more extensive approaches must be taken to characterize individuals who are excluded (rather than just noting the number of participants who were excluded). Suggested characteristics to document include age, sex, global cognitive level, autistic traits, adaptive behavior, and maladaptive behavior.The goal of such documentation is to increase transparency about the generalizability of the findings -i.e., to whom research findings apply and perhaps more importantly, to whom they do not apply. This documentation may provide the necessary scientific justification for the development of alternative technologies that fit the needs of participants with NDDs for whom existing approaches are not appropriate. It is hoped that this will increase access to research, and in turn, will increase equity in accessing interventions for all individuals with NDDs.Figure 1. Barriers to magnetic resonance imaging for neurodevelopmental disorders and the promise of portable neuroimaging methods Panel a illustrates barriers of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), how these barriers impact individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) in particular, and how portable neurotechnologies such as functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) or electroencephalography (EEG) may help to reduce barriers. Panel b presents an example of how fNIRS can be used in a child's natural environment to reduce the impact of the barriers presented in panel a.Abbreviations: EEG=electroencephalography; fNIRS= functional near infrared spectroscopy; MRI=magnetic resonance imaging; NDDs=neurodevelopmental disorders
authors: Nancy Lee

title: Ultrasound neuromodulation in brain disorders: from mechanotransduction mechanisms to clinical translation
abstract: Brain disorders impose a major global health burden, yet current pharmacological and neuromodulation therapies are often constrained by invasiveness, limited spatial precision, poor access to deep brain structures, or insufficient long-term efficacy. Non-invasive ultrasound neuromodulation has emerged as a promising approach combining high spatial resolution, deep tissue penetration, and reversible modulation. Its biological effects arise from multiscale mechanotransduction involving membrane deformation, mechanosensitive ion channels, intracellular calcium signaling, glial regulation, and neurovascular coupling. Together, these processes modulate neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, network connectivity, neuroinflammation, and cerebral perfusion. Preclinical studies support its therapeutic potential across neurological and psychiatric disorders, while early clinical studies indicate short-term tolerability and preliminary target engagement in Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and depression. Emerging approaches, including individualized treatment planning, closed-loop stimulation, and sonogenetics, may further improve the precision and cellular specificity of ultrasound neuromodulation. This review summarizes the physical principles and cellular mechanisms of ultrasound neuromodulation, evaluates its therapeutic and clinical applications, and discusses key challenges and future directions, including personalized stimulation, closed-loop systems, sonogenetics, and disease-modifying strategies.
authors: Rufei Zhang, Li Li, Jinzhong Tang, Si Hu, Qin Zhang et al.

title: The Unified Catastrophic Cascade and the Law of Pressure Reflection: A Capstone Synthesis of the Brain's Miser Economy, the Multi-Blade Arsenal, and the Clinical Gauge
abstract: Background: The preceding papers of this framework have established that the brain's primary function is the maintenance of temperature and blood pH through the control of blood flow. Under perceived threat, the brain becomes a miser—it constricts peripheral vessels, hoards blood centrally, and sacrifices non-essential territories. This single decree, executed through the multi-blade arsenal of thermal, vascular, immune, metabolic, postural, behavioural, cognitive, neurochemical, and emotional defences, explains the vast landscape of chronic disease now split into separate specialties. The Stasis-Acidosis-Proteinopathy (SAP) cascade transforms vascular constriction into tissue damage and rational immune attack. The Universal Brain Threat Index (UBTI) and its Ocular UBTI extension provide quantitative, real-time readouts of the brain's defensive state. The GLP-1/PDE5 starter motor offers a time-limited pharmacological override, calibrated to the thickness of the brain's defensive wall. The Golden First Hour identifies birth as the earliest modifiable calibration window. This framework is a bold hypothesis, but it is built on solid ground. The fragmentation of the human body into isolated organs and specialties does not stand a chance of achieving rectification or cure, because the brain does not think in organs. It thinks in survival. And survival is always total. The paper therefore emphasises a right-side-up, cohesive understanding of the brain and body as one system under one decree. Every disease described in this series is a station on one line. Every symptom is a blade of one arsenal. Every therapy must be judged by one question: does it lower the UBTI and tell the brain that the war is over? Objective: This capstone synthesises these components into a single catastrophic cascade: the trajectory from the first knock to the final scar equilibrium. It names the central principle governing the entire framework—the Law of Pressure Reflection—which states that suppression of one defensive blade, without resolution of the underlying threat, displaces the brain's protective pressure into other blades, other territories, and other timescales. This law unifies the clinical observation that symptom-targeted therapies often fail or produce new symptoms, and it defines the criterion for genuine healing: the lowering of the UBTI and the voluntary withdrawal of the brain's decree. Framework: The capstone presents the Unified Catastrophic Cascade as a sequence of eleven stations: (1) the knock, (2) the gate, (3) the decree, (4) the SAP cascade, (5) the first sacrifice, (6) the flickering gate, (7) the metabolic throttle, (8) the inflamed territory, (9) the exhausted brain, (10) the frozen frame, and (11) the final scar. It integrates the Indestructible Engram as the physical basis for why the brain cannot simply "let go" of past threats, and the Rosehip Sentinel as the cellular structure that translates early environmental data into lifelong gating. It explains hyperthyroidism, ADHD, dry eye, thyroid disease, neurodegeneration, vitiligo, liver disease, and autoimmune disease as points on the same line. It incorporates the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) as the universal survival molecule at the molecular core of the UBTI, and it demonstrates that the bold-lettered contraindications on every drug label are the documented map of the Law of Pressure Reflection. Clinical Integration: The capstone specifies the therapeutic order: measure the UBTI, assess wall thickness, quiet the knock, apply the starter motor only when needed, and taper when the brain stands down. It defines the endpoint of healing not as normalisation of a single laboratory value, but as a brain that has verified safety through both chemical and physical thresholds and has voluntarily relaxed its grip. It argues that the present medical system, by treating each station as a separate disease, is itself a victim of the cascade it fails to see. The Ocular UBTI is the tool that finally makes the cascade visible, and the environmental path is the only sustainable cure. Conclusion: The framework is complete. The brain is a miser, the knock is relentless, and the diseases of modernity are the predictable, logical output of a brain doing exactly what it was designed to do in an environment it never evolved to inhabit. The Law of Pressure Reflection is the final unifying principle. When the medical fraternity learns to read the UBTI, to respect vascular sovereignty, and to quiet the knock, it will have moved from a fragmented symptom economy to a right-side-up understanding of the brain. Keywords: Law of Pressure Reflection; unified catastrophic cascade; UBTI; Ocular UBTI; SAP cascade; multi-blade arsenal; brain miser; vascular sovereignty; starter motor; GLP-1; PDE5; rosehip sentinel; indestructible engram; golden first hour; environmental path; ADHD; thyroid gland; vitiligo; liver; Parkinson's disease; Alzheimer's; autoimmune disease; APP; homeostasis

title: Serotonergic circuit architecture underlies sex dimorphism in anxiogenic states
abstract: ABSTRACT The serotonergic system underpins anxiety-like behavior vital for the adaptive response to a new environment. However, our understanding of the neural circuitry underlying the diversity of anxiety-like behaviors across individuals is limited. Whilst previous studies have characterized diverse features related to the neurochemical substrate of serotonergic neurotransmission and behavioral presentation between males and females, no investigations have fully addressed the sexual dimorphism in the structural and functional connectivity of serotonergic circuits. Here, using functional FosTRAP connectivity analysis, we found sex-dependent functional differences in the serotonergic neurons of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), such as enriched connectivity to the amygdala in females, compared to male mice. We also discovered previously unidentified morpho-functional sex-specific differences in DRN serotonergic circuitry that reflects the disparity in behavior presentation. To understand the molecular basis of serotonergic circuit architecture differences between sexes, we leveraged on single-cell RNA sequencing dataset from DRN serotonergic cells taking sex as a biological variable and spotted some gene candidates involved in neural circuit wiring. Altering the expression of the receptor tyrosine kinase Erbb4 in serotonergic circuits, altered the axonal connectivity to downstream targets and shifted sex-specific behavior. Overall, this study provides an essential foundation to delineate the molecular basis and connectivity pattern mechanisms underlying the serotonergic system-dependent sex-specific anxiety behavior. Since alterations in serotonin function play a vital role in adaptive behavior, as well as various pathologies including chronic anxiety and depression, this study may advance our understanding of sex-biases in presentation and treatment response of neuropsychiatric disorders. Breakthroughs of this work We identified structural sex-specific features of serotonergic innervation from the DRN and revealed molecular determinants of sex-dimorphic serotonergic connectivity. Teaser Sex dimorphism in anxiety is shaped by distinct connectivity patterns and molecular programs within serotonergic circuits in mice.
authors: Noorya Yasmin Ahmed, Yillcer Molina, Álvaro Ballesteros González, Alicia Juan, William C. Kwan et al.

title: The Origins and Mechanisms of Auditory and Motor Rhythm Entrainment: Behavioral, Neuroimaging, and Psychophysical Investigations
abstract: Humans and parrots are, among animals, uniquely able to move in time with a musical beat—a capacity termed beat perception and synchronization (BPS). Both are also advanced vocal learners, which has led to the proposal that BPS emerged as a by-product of the neural machinery for complex vocal learning. This dissertation examines rhythmic auditory-motor entrainment across three experiments, asking both where this capacity comes from and whether perceiving a rhythm itself engages the motor system.The first experiment tested a behavioral prediction of this speech-origin account: if rhythmic synchronization is grounded in the speech system, the vocal system should be at least as good at it as a non-vocal effector. Participants synchronized to isochronous rhythms at varying rates by finger tapping or by tongue clicking, a supralaryngeal vocal effector. Tongue clicking was as consistent as finger tapping and, on average, more closely aligned to the beat, leaving the speech-origin premise intact.The second experiment mapped the neural substrate of the same comparison with fMRI, asking whether the two effectors are served by segregated circuits or by a shared component. Beyond the expected effector-specific regions, finger and tongue synchronization converged on common cortex, most notably the dorsal precentral speech area (dPCSA), an auditory-weighted region of the speech-coordination network. Because the task involved no pitch or laryngeal control, the engagement of the dPCSA suggests it is not modality-specific but multifunctional—an auditory-weighted region within the motor system that may act as a common node for auditory-motor synchronization across effectors.The third experiment turned from the effectors of synchronization to the mechanism of perception, testing the motor theory of rhythm—the claim that perceiving a rhythm depends on covertly simulating it motorically. Using a forward-entrainment paradigm, the auditory rhythm was removed and participants generated the rhythm by tapping, a design that predicts an at-least-as-strong perceptual after-effect if the motor system is its source. A subset of participants showed a modulation of the expected magnitude, but the enhancement predicted by the motor account was not observed, and the pattern was not consistently phase-aligned across participants; the results are therefore inconclusive, neither confirming nor excluding a motor contribution.Together, these experiments support a speech-based origin for rhythmic synchronization and reveal a shared, auditory-weighted cortical substrate for it across vocal and non-vocal effectors, while leaving open whether rhythm perception itself depends on motor simulation.
authors: Jie Wan

title: Predictive coding unifies neural and behavioral signatures of contextual facilitation
abstract: During comprehension, words that are primed or predictable are processed more quickly and elicit smaller N400 responses than words that are less consistent with their preceding context. Although these behavioral and neural effects are both commonly interpreted as evidence of facilitated processing, they have typically been explained within different computational frameworks that impose seemingly conflicting constraints: behavioral facilitation requires more activity to accumulate over expected representations, allowing a decision threshold to be reached earlier, whereas N400 facilitation requires less neural activity to be generated overall. Here, we show that an implemented model of predictive coding provides a unified mechanistic account of both phenomena and, in doing so, resolves three longstanding puzzles. First, it explains how facilitated processing can simultaneously produce faster behavioral responses and reduced neural activity: expected representations accumulate activity more rapidly in state units while generating less activity in error units. Second, an asymmetry between top-down priors and bottom-up evidence allows context to pre-activate multiple lexical candidates without inducing premature competition or misprediction costs. Third, it reconciles apparently conflicting claims about the timing of contextual facilitation by showing that behavioral and neural measures can reflect different phases along a single continuous trajectory of lexico-semantic processing, rather than distinct processing stages.
authors: Samer Nour Eddine, Anthony Yacovone, Gina R. Kuperberg

title: Electrophysiological properties of the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus motoneurones controlling airway mucus secretion in rats
abstract: Abstract The parasympathetic efferent innervation to the respiratory airways controls bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion. It is known that the parasympathetic respiratory motoneurones (PRMNs) projecting to the airways are located in the nucleus ambiguus (NA) and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV). Although NA PRMNs are known to regulate bronchoconstriction in both physiological and pathological conditions, the electrophysiological properties of DMV PRMNs and their functional role in regulating the airways are not entirely clear. Retrograde labelling, neuronal and ventilatory recordings, optogenetics, chemogenetics, and histological and molecular analyses in vitro and in vivo preparations of rats were performed to evaluate the electrophysiological characteristics controlling the activity of DMV PRMNs and their role in airway mucus secretion. DMV PRMNs present K + ‐dominated leak currents, mediated by two‐pore domain TWIK‐2 channels, which regulate their resting membrane potential, firing frequency and excitation by acidosis. Acidosis also reduces synaptic inhibition to these motoneurones and activates astrocytes in the DMV. Furthermore, optogenetic activation of astrocytes induced action potentials in DMV PRMNs, mediated by glutamatergic NMDA receptor excitation. Finally, chemogenetic activation of DMV PRMNs evoked mucus secretion in respiratory airways and increases sighing, without affecting inflammatory cell infiltration, pulmonary ventilation, oxygen consumption or heart rate. Therefore, our data demonstrate that TWIK‐2 leak channels and astrocytes signalling regulate the activity of DMV PRMNs and their role in airway mucus secretion of rats. image Key points Parasympathetic respiratory motoneurones (PRMNs) of the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV) present K+‐dominated leak currents, mediated by TWIK‐2 channels, regulating their resting membrane potential, firing frequency and excitation by acidosis. Acidosis also reduces synaptic inhibition to DMV PRMNs and activates astrocytes in the DMV. Activation of DMV astrocytes induced action potentials in PRMNs, mediated by glutamatergic NMDA receptor excitation. Activation of DMV PRMNs evoked mucus secretion in respiratory airways and increased sighing, without affecting pulmonary ventilation, oxygen consumption or heart rate. TWIK‐2 leak channels and astrocytes signalling regulate the activity of DMV PRMNs and their role in airway mucus secretion of rats.
authors: Daniel P. de Souza, Renato Willian Martins Sá, Luiza Henrique de Souza, Fernando S. Ramalho, Davi J. A. Moraes

title: Pre-Existing Serotonergic Pathways Guide the Navigation of Developing Serotonergic Axons
abstract: Abstract The serotonergic system originates from a small population of brainstem neurons whose axons form one of the most extensive projection networks in the vertebrate nervous system. Although a number of molecular regulators of serotonergic development have been identified, the core principles that organize this widespread axonal architecture remain poorly understood. Classical neuroanatomical studies have proposed that serotonergic axons may navigate by growing along pre-existing fiber tracts, a process termed epiphytic guidance, but this hypothesis has remained largely untested. Here, we used organotypic transplantation assays to investigate how embryonic serotonergic axons navigate within developing and adult neural tissue. Rostral raphe explants from Tph2-GFP embryos were grafted onto embryonic hindbrain flat-mounts or adult brain slices, allowing donor-derived axons to be visualized in relation to genetically labelled endogenous serotonergic pathways and host tissue architecture. Across different grafting configurations, developmental stages, and both homotopic and heterotopic host territories, donor-derived axons consistently aligned with pre-existing serotonergic pathways adopting local trajectories rather than growing independently of them. This substrate-dependent behavior extended to adult tissue, where transplanted embryonic axons preferentially followed pre-existing serotonergic axon directions. These observations reveal substantial navigational plasticity and indicate that axonal and tissue architectures can provide permissive and potentially instructive substrates for the dispersal of serotonergic fibers. Together, our findings provide experimental support for epiphytic guidance and suggest that serotonergic pathway assembly relies, at least in part, on a pioneer-follower mechanism of progressive self-scaffolding. Such a strategy may help explain how a small population of raphe neurons generates an extensive and spatially coherent neuromodulatory system.
authors: Marta Picchi, Sara Migliarini, Serena Nazzi, Giulia Gianni, Skirmantas Janušonis et al.

title: Dose-Dependent Effects of Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound on Human Deep White Matter Tracts
abstract: Background: Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is emerging as a method for anatomically specific, noninvasive, and reversible neuromodulation of deep brain structures relevant to psychopathology. A key requirement for clinical translation is evidence of graded target engagement. We examined whether LIFU applied to deep white matter tracts produces dose-dependent functional connectivity changes in healthy adults. Methods: , 0.5 MHz, in a θ-burst pattern) of individually modeled right thalamo-prefrontal white matter tracts under two dose conditions: one and three consecutive sonications. Dose-dependent changes in resting-state functional connectivity were examined during a 30-minute poststimulation period in 31 participants. Results: One sonication acutely increased right thalamic functional connectivity with the left thalamus (28 voxels; Z = 5.48, Cohen's d = 0.61), whereas three sonications decreased connectivity with the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Z = -4.05, Cohen's d = -0.45). Poststimulation time-course analysis revealed a 3-LIFU-specific linear recovery trend in the left cerebellum (Z = 4.14, d = 0.48), reflecting initial suppression followed by progressive recovery across 30 minutes. Stronger thalamo-prefrontal structural connectivity was associated with condition-specific functional connectivity changes (left frontal pole; F = 14.73, ηp² = 0.41). Conclusions: These findings provide initial human evidence that LIFU is well tolerated and produces dose-dependent changes in functional connectivity associated with deep white matter tract stimulation, informing parameter selection for future circuit-based mechanistic and clinical studies.
